result: NOT ADOPTED (strict count): round 1 Yes 1 (developer), Support-it 4 (product manager, architect, QA, decider), No 1 (audit lens, no cite); the architect's cite did not match (capital letter) and was re-asked; amended (C6b) for the audit lens's condition; D187 re-ask of the architect and the audit lens alone: architect Support-it (cite verbatim), audit lens No again with a new condition (a complete snapshot authenticated against immutable source evidence from git alone), unresolved after the amendment, so the proposal fails. round1.cite: The 60 minutes is a number to review at the trial's retro, not a standing rule.
round1.reply:
Support-it

The proposal resolves the architect's one condition and adds nothing else (D145). It also serves the product owner's accountability rule: decisions are acknowledged in a committed log and checked against a metric. It keeps the Decider protocol exactly as written and keeps the board unchanged. The script must go red before green, and the trial counts only from the card after it lands, so the rule isn't judged before its check exists.

My concern is over-specification (VISION ruling 6). Six rejection rules and a 60-minute threshold are a lot for a file-read experiment. The 60 minutes is explicitly open to review, and counter-metric 4 flags more than 5 minutes per boundary as ceremony. That is acceptable for a three-card trial.

CITE: The 60 minutes is a number to review at the trial's retro, not a standing rule.

round1.cite: the script rejects: a log line with a missing field;
with a committed log and a script that checks the log mechanically
round1.reply:
Support-it

C6 is red-first testable with isolated fixtures for every named rejection, including inbox reconciliation. The checker must parse timestamps strictly and test boundary values at exactly 60 minutes, duplicate IDs, nonexistent paths, and acknowledged headings absent from the log. A passing state can still cite an unrelated existing repository path, so destination existence proves presence, not semantic correctness; acceptable for a three-card experiment, but the retro should inspect this gap. “Fixed or explained” must not turn a rejected log into a successful check.

round1.cite: with a committed log and a script that checks the log mechanically
round1.reply:
Support-it

The experiment is evidence-ready: immutable IDs, timestamps, boundaries, destinations, failure cases, baseline, target, counter-metrics, and a three-card decision point support keep/revise/drop. C6 resolves the prior architect’s condition without changing the channel. The full set of product, architecture, QA, implementation, audit, Decider, and coaching seats is represented. At the final retro, distinguish script compliance from actual delivery: an accepted log line and existing destination prove routing, not that the decision reached and influenced the team.

CITE: with a committed log and a script that checks the log mechanically

round2_reask.cite: The script cross-validates the two committed files, so it no longer needs the external file
round2_reask.reply:
Support-it

The design resolves my D191 condition. Entry identity is a hash of the heading, and the boundary is recorded in git. The script mechanically rejects missing, duplicate, late and destination-less lines. The snapshot file makes the check run on committed data alone, and the append-only comparison against `git show HEAD:` is enforceable.

Two residual risks, neither blocking:
- A renamed heading changes `entry_id`, which could cause false positives.
- A `destination` that is a card or closure record rather than a file path needs a defined mapping, or the "path exists" rule will misfire.

Settle both during the red-then-green tests.

CITE: The script cross-validates the two committed files, so it no longer needs the external file

round2_reask.cite: Each boundary commit that touches the log also appends
round2_reask.reply:
No

Git cannot prove that each snapshot contains every external inbox heading: an omitted entry can remain absent from both committed files, letting the checker and metric pass while C1–C2 are broken. I would vote yes if each boundary commits a mechanically produced, complete snapshot authenticated against immutable source evidence that later audits can verify from git alone.

CITE: Each boundary commit that touches the log also appends
